scenes.headline: Concurrency & Parallelism
scenes.subtitle: Doing more at once in data pipelines
scenes.narration: Concurrency and parallelism are the two levers you pull to make a data pipeline do more in less wall-clock time, and choosing between them correctly is one of the most impactful decisions in performance engineering.

scenes.headline: Concurrency vs Parallelism

columns.title: Parallelism
points: Runs tasks at the same instant

scenes.narration: Concurrency is about structure: it interleaves tasks so that while one is waiting on the network or disk, another can make progress. Parallelism is about execution: it literally runs computations at the same moment across multiple cores. Reach for concurrency when your bottleneck is waiting, and parallelism when your bottleneck is calculating.

scenes.headline: Python's three tools
items: threading — many threads sharing memory, but GIL-bound for CPU work
multiprocessing — separate processes that achieve real parallelism
asyncio — a cooperative single-threaded event loop for high-concurrency I/O
scenes.narration: The threading module gives you lightweight threads that share memory, but the Global Interpreter Lock prevents them from speeding up CPU-bound code. The multiprocessing module spawns independent processes, each with its own interpreter, so heavy computation truly runs in parallel. asyncio offers a single-threaded event loop that juggles thousands of I/O operations with minimal overhead.

scenes.headline: Choosing the model
scenes.narration: Start by asking whether your task spends its time waiting or calculating. If it is waiting on APIs, files, or databases, threads or asyncio let those waits overlap. If it is crunching numbers, only multiprocessing escapes the GIL and puts every core to work.

scenes.headline: I/O-bound: ThreadPoolExecutor
scenes.code:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
import requests

urls = [f"https://api.example.com/rows/{i}" for i in range(50)]

def fetch(url):
    return requests.get(url, timeout=10).json()

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(fetch, urls))
scenes.narration: Here a ThreadPoolExecutor manages a pool of ten worker threads. The pool.map call hands each URL to a free thread, and because each fetch spends most of its time waiting on the network, the GIL is released during that wait. The result is that fifty requests overlap, so total latency approaches the slowest single request rather than the sum of all fifty.

scenes.headline: CPU-bound: ProcessPoolExecutor
scenes.code:
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

def transform(chunk):
    return sum(x * x for x in chunk)

chunks = [range(i, i + 100000) for i in range(0, 1000000, 100000)]

with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool:
    totals = list(pool.map(transform, chunks))
    print(sum(totals))
scenes.narration: This example splits a million numbers into ten chunks and hands each to a ProcessPoolExecutor. Because every worker runs in its own interpreter process, there is no shared GIL to serialize them, so the squaring work genuinely runs across multiple cores. The trade-off is that inputs and outputs must be pickled and shipped between processes, which only pays off when the computation is substantial.

scenes.headline: Common pitfalls
items: Using threads for CPU work, where the GIL silently blocks any speedup
Sharing mutable state across threads without locks, inviting race conditions
Ignoring the pickling and startup cost of spawning processes
scenes.narration: The classic mistake is throwing threads at CPU-bound code and wondering why nothing gets faster. Sharing mutable objects between threads without locks quietly corrupts state through race conditions. And spinning up processes for tiny tasks can cost more in serialization overhead than the work itself saves.

scenes.text: I/O-bound work belongs to threads or asyncio; CPU-bound work belongs to multiprocessing. Always match the model to the bottleneck.
scenes.narration: The golden rule is to identify your bottleneck first: overlap waiting with threads or asyncio, and spread computation with processes. Match the concurrency model to the problem and performance follows naturally.
